1.concept: A circular linked list is a linked list where the last node's `next` points back to the first node instead of to NULL, forming a loop by design. This is different from a 'cyclic bug' — an accidental loop caused by a mistake — even though both look similar on a diagram. One is intentional; the other is broken. The visual treatment of each must never be confused. The practical consequence: traversal can no longer rely on hitting NULL to know it's done, since there is no NULL to hit. Code has to track termination another way — usually by stopping once it revisits the starting node, or by keeping an explicit count. This structure shows up anywhere a system needs to cycle indefinitely without a natural endpoint, like round-robin CPU scheduling or a playlist set to repeat.
1.analogy: Imagine a circular train line versus a train that accidentally got routed back to a station it already passed. Both loop — but one was built to loop on purpose (a scheduled circuit), and the other is a routing mistake that will run forever without ever reaching its actual destination.
1.mascotDialogue: A circular list looping is a feature. The exact same shape appearing by accident is a bug. Same picture, opposite meaning — so we render them in different colors, on purpose.

2.mascotDialogue: Line 6 is the design choice. Line 13 is the consequence: you can never check `curr != NULL` to stop, because NULL never appears in a circular list. You have to check `curr != head` instead.

3.mascotDialogue: That last arrow, c back to a, is drawn in the calm closed-loop color — this loop is supposed to be here.

4.bugDescription: c->next was meant to either terminate the list (NULL) or wrap fully back to a (circular). Instead it points to b, creating an unintended loop between b and c. Any traversal starting at a will run forever, alternating b, c, b, c, and will never reach a again.
4.mascotDialogue: See the difference? That arrow is drawn in the warning color, not the calm loop color — because this loop was never supposed to exist, and traversal will spin on it forever without warning.

5.question: What visually distinguishes an intentional circular list from a cyclic bug in this app?
5.answer: They use different colors/styling even though the pointer shape is identical
hints: The two states can have the exact same arrow layout.
SeeDS 2.0 was rebuilt specifically to fix confusion between these two states — see structureVariant.
5.solution: structureVariant is set explicitly to 'circular' or 'cyclic-bug', and each renders with a distinct color/treatment (calm green closed-loop vs. warning red) — the pointer shapes can be identical, but the meaning and visual treatment must never be confused.
